title: Clomipramine tops OCD drugs, a pan-cancer tumour atlas, and a null organoid trial
dek: A 52-trial analysis ranks OCD drugs by benefit and cost. A Nature atlas finds shared stromal programmes across 42 cancers. Also: a hidden inherited prostate cancer gene, why psychiatric biomarkers fail, and a transposon behind a movement disorder.

tldr.text: In 52 trials with 7,316 people, clomipramine eased OCD most in adults (SMD -0.71) but was also the hardest to tolerate.
Single-cell data from more than 2,000 tumours across 42 cancer types show shared stromal and immune programmes in people and mice.
In a phase 3 trial in metastatic pancreatic cancer, organoid-guided treatment gave 8.6 versus 8.7 months median survival, so no benefit overall.
Five men with metastatic prostate cancer carried an inherited CDK12 fault, among 4,535 tested.
A JAMA Psychiatry paper says most psychiatric biomarkers fail outside the study that found them, and shows how to test them more fairly.

top.title: Clomipramine eases OCD most, but is harder to tolerate than other drugs
top.gist: A pooled analysis of 52 trials (7,316 people) compared OCD drugs against placebo and each other. Clomipramine helped most, but more people stopped taking it because of side effects.

evidence.limitation: Short trials (8 to 16 weeks). Only 9 trials were in children, and most of that evidence was rated low or very low certainty.

top.why: OCD drugs are rarely compared head to head. This ranks them in adults and in children and says plainly how sure the evidence is, which matters for shared decisions.
details: In adults (43 trials, 6,494 people), clomipramine beat placebo with a standardised mean difference of -0.71 (95% CI -0.88 to -0.54), rated high certainty. Fluvoxamine (-0.63), paroxetine (-0.51), sertraline (-0.49), escitalopram (-0.43) and fluoxetine (-0.37) also beat placebo, mostly at moderate certainty.

Clomipramine was also less tolerable than placebo (odds of stopping because of side effects 4.65, 95% CI 3.27 to 6.60). In children and adolescents (9 trials, 822 people) it looked even stronger against SSRIs, but the certainty was low or very low.

People with lived experience of OCD took part in every stage of the review, and the protocol was preregistered. The authors suggest the trade-off between benefit and tolerability should be discussed in shared decision making.
top.didNotShow: It did not show long-term outcomes, results for psychotherapy, or that clomipramine is best for any one person.

terms.def: A method that pools many trials to compare several treatments, even pairs never tested head to head.
Standardised mean difference, a score that puts results from different symptom scales on one comparable scale.
An older antidepressant from the tricyclic family, used for obsessive-compulsive disorder.
A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, a common class of antidepressant such as sertraline or fluoxetine.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder, a condition with intrusive thoughts and repeated behaviours.

sources.label: The Lancet Psychiatry, Cohen et al.

top.forYou: Evidence synthesis and certainty grading relevant to any comparative drug question.

top.title: Tumour surroundings share conserved programmes across 42 cancer types and two species
top.gist: Screening thousands of public single-cell datasets, a Nature study found shared stromal and immune programmes in more than 2,000 human and mouse tumours, and released a free atlas and software.

evidence.limitation: Re-analysis of public datasets. It shows what is shared across tumours, not which programme causes disease or could be treated.

top.why: Most tumour microenvironment work studies one cancer at a time. A shared, reusable map lets labs check whether a finding in one tumour holds in others.
details: The authors algorithmically screened public single-cell RNA datasets for signatures of stromal (supporting) and immune cells across tissues and species.
The results are packaged as an interactive web atlas (tmeatlas.stanford.edu) and a software package called scTME, so other groups can query them.
top.didNotShow: The abstract does not show which shared programmes drive tumour growth or resistance, or whether any can be targeted.

terms.def: The cells, fibres and signals around a tumour that support or fight it.
Describes data that measure which genes are active in each individual cell.
Describes the supporting tissue cells, such as fibroblasts, that surround a tumour.

top.forYou: A reusable stroma and immune reference relevant to dense-stroma tumour work.

top.title: Organoid-guided treatment did not extend survival in metastatic pancreatic cancer
top.gist: A review of the AVATAR phase 3 trial says personalised drug testing on tumour organoids gave no survival gain overall, because most patients were too unwell to receive a matched drug.

evidence.limitation: A narrative review of one trial. The 4-patient matched subgroup is not randomised, so its long survival is only a hint.

top.why: Pancreatic cancer has few treatment options. This shows that a good lab test can still fail in the clinic when it takes too long.
details: The review reports a median overall survival of 8.6 versus 8.7 months (p = 0.849), so no intention-to-treat benefit. Of 39 experimental-arm patients who went on to later lines, 35 received no matched therapy, and clinical deterioration was the leading reason (26 patients).

The 4 patients (10 percent) who did get matched therapy reached a median survival of 19.3 months. The author calls this exploratory and says the main limit is speed from biopsy to treatment, not the lab model itself.
The review also covers organoids grown together with stroma, and combinations of new KRAS inhibitors against resistance.
top.didNotShow: It did not show that organoid-matched therapy works. The review is not a new trial, and the matched group was only four people.

terms.def: A tiny three-dimensional culture grown from a patient's tumour cells that mimics the tumour in the dish.
An analysis that counts every patient in the group they were assigned to, whatever treatment they finally received.
A gene that is mutated in most pancreatic cancers and drives tumour growth.
The name of a phase 3 trial of personalised drug choice in metastatic pancreatic cancer.

nodes.note: Reached a later line of treatment

diagram.caption: In the AVATAR experimental arm, only 4 of 39 patients who reached a later line received an organoid-matched therapy.

sources.label: Drug Design, Development and Therapy, Alsaikhan (review)

top.forYou: Organoid pharmacotyping and time-to-treatment constraints relevant to pancreatic cancer models.

top.title: Inherited CDK12 faults found in five men with metastatic prostate cancer
top.gist: Among 4,535 men with aggressive prostate cancer tested, five (0.1 percent), aged 44 to 62, carried an inherited CDK12 fault, a gene thought to change only inside tumours.

evidence.limitation: Very few cases. Population control comparisons come from public databases, not matched men.

top.why: If confirmed, some families could be offered earlier screening. It also shows a gene seen as tumour-only can be inherited.
details: All five tumours also had a second CDK12 fault and a typical pattern of hundreds of tandem duplications. The inherited faults were more common in metastatic prostate cancer than in public control groups (odds ratio 11.4 against one database, 95% CI 3.6 to 27.8).

Family histories included prostate and ovarian cancers, and inheritance was confirmed in the two families tested. The paper appeared online in July 2026, and a university release on 17 November brought it back into the news.
top.didNotShow: It did not show how risky the inherited fault is for a carrier, or that screening carriers saves lives.

terms.def: Describes a genetic change present in every cell from birth and passed to children.
Describes a genetic change that arises later in a tumour and is not inherited.
A copying error in which a piece of DNA is repeated next to itself.
A gene that is mutated in some metastatic prostate cancers.

top.forYou: Germline testing and tumour mutational signatures relevant to cancer genetics.

top.title: Most psychiatric biomarkers fail outside the study that found them
top.gist: A psychiatry journal paper reviews six depression biomarker studies against five unreliable practices, and says even modern methods repeat them. It proposes fairer internal validation.

evidence.limitation: A small illustrative sample of depression studies, and the abstract gives no full list of the five principles.

top.why: Many brain-scan and blood marker claims in psychiatry never replicate. Knowing the common traps helps readers judge new claims.
details: The authors say well-documented unreliable practices have contributed to failed biomarker research, and that complex data augmentation, synthetic data and cross-validation can still hide them.
They set out alternative strategies for rigorous internal validation to improve replicability.
top.didNotShow: It did not test any single biomarker, or show how often these practices occur across all psychiatric research.

terms.def: A measurable sign, such as a blood level or brain scan pattern, that points to a condition or treatment response.
Testing a finding on new people from a different study to see if it holds.
A way to test a model by repeatedly training it on part of the data and checking it on the rest.

top.forYou: Validation discipline relevant to any biomarker or imaging study.

top.title: Adenomyosis may lower live birth after IVF, and treatment evidence is thin
top.gist: A Fertility and Sterility review says adenomyosis is under-recognised, IVF may have fewer live births in affected women, and pre-IVF drug treatments lack consistent evidence.

evidence.limitation: A review of mostly observational studies, with confounders. The abstract gives no pooled numbers.

top.why: Adenomyosis often goes with endometriosis and can affect fertility. Clear gaps in evidence show where trials are needed.
details: The review notes that new ultrasound criteria (MUSA) and its link to endometriosis changed understanding of the disease. Surgery is invasive and can recur, and hormonal drugs prevent conception and have not helped infertility.

Studies of GnRH agonists, dienogest or levonorgestrel intrauterine systems before IVF are described as insufficient and inconsistent. The authors call for randomised trials with standard inclusion criteria.
top.didNotShow: It did not show that any pre-IVF treatment improves live birth.

terms.def: A condition in which womb lining tissue grows into the muscular wall of the womb.
Agreed ultrasound features used to diagnose adenomyosis.
A drug that switches off the body's own sex hormone signals, sometimes used before IVF.
In vitro fertilisation, in which eggs are fertilised in a lab and the embryo is placed in the womb.

sources.label: Fertility and Sterility, Somigliana et al.

top.title: Age hurt IVF egg and embryo quality most, while endometriosis and obesity showed no consistent loss
top.gist: In 1,856 ICSI cycles (14,420 eggs), maternal age gave the clearest decline in embryo outcomes. An AI egg score modestly improved prediction across groups.

evidence.limitation: A retrospective cohort from one setting, with an AI score that added only modest prediction beyond clinical factors.

top.why: It separates how different fertility factors act on egg quality, rather than treating them as one problem, and tests a computer score for eggs.
details: Endometriosis and obesity were not linked to consistent drops, while overweight was linked to fewer top-quality blastocysts and lower cumulative outcomes. PMOS cycles kept largely normal lab outcomes.
The composite MAGENTA score tracked fertilisation (OR 1.53), blastocyst formation (OR 1.67) and top-quality blastocyst formation (OR 1.26).
top.didNotShow: It did not show cause and effect, or that using the AI score improves live births.

terms.def: A form of IVF in which a single sperm is injected directly into an egg.
A developing egg cell.
An early embryo at about day five or six, ready to implant.
Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, a condition involving hormones, metabolism and the ovaries.

sources.label: Frontiers in Endocrinology, Del Collado et al.

top.forYou: Retrospective cohort methods and AI scoring relevant to reproductive data.

bench.title: Genome writing reveals SVA retrotransposon consequences in X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism
bench.headline: A jumping-gene insertion inside the TAF1 gene lowers a key TAF1 transcript and kills cells. In mice it caused striatal shrinkage and early death in males.
bench.authors: Zhang W, Zhao Y, Prakash P, et al.

evidence.model: Mouse embryonic stem cells and mice carrying a 78-kb human XDP TAF1 allele
evidence.limitation: Mouse models. Read from the abstract only, so group sizes and effect sizes were not checked.

bench.question: How does the SVA insertion in the TAF1 gene cause the neurodegeneration of X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP)?
bench.approach: The team rewrote a section of the mouse Taf1 gene with the matching 78-kb human patient sequence, with and without the SVA, and studied cells and mice.
bench.model: Mouse embryonic stem cells, and mice with the human patient allele in neuron-lineage cells.
bench.result: The SVA itself, not the hybrid gene structure, lowered hybrid TAF1 mRNA. Genes with TATA boxes fell and cells died. The SVA is transcribed and seems to block transcription. Male mice died within 2 months and showed striatal atrophy. Switching on hybrid TAF1 with CRISPRa restored cell survival.
bench.limitations: Mouse model, abstract only. Lethality in mice does not match human timing, and the therapy idea was shown in stem cells, not animals.
bench.meaning: Boosting TAF1 transcription is a possible route for XDP, and genome writing offers a way to study large human insertions.

diagram.caption: In the mouse models, the SVA insertion lowers hybrid TAF1 mRNA, which downregulates TATA-box genes and triggers cell death.

terms.def: A stretch of DNA that can copy itself and insert into new places in the genome.
SINE-VNTR-Alu, a human-specific type of retrotransposon.
A CRISPR method that switches a gene on without cutting DNA.
A deep brain region that helps control movement.

bench.forYou: Large-insert genome engineering and transcription-elongation biology relevant to rare neurodegeneration.

bench.title: Targeting cancer immune evasion with anti-FOLR1 antibody-drug conjugate potentiates anti-PD-1 efficacy in colorectal cancer
bench.headline: In mice, a drug already used against FOLR1-positive tumours reawakened immune attack on colorectal cancer when combined with an anti-PD-1 antibody.
bench.authors: Chen S, Liu Q, Ye S, et al.

evidence.model: Colorectal cancer cell lines, patient tumour data and mouse models
evidence.limitation: Preclinical. Read from the abstract only, so sample sizes and effect sizes were not checked.

bench.question: Why do some colorectal tumours lose MHC-I and escape immunotherapy, and can the cause be drugged?
bench.approach: A genome-wide CRISPR activation screen sorted cells by MHC-I level. Follow-up work traced the mechanism, then tested the antibody-drug conjugate mirvetuximab soravtansine (IMGN853) with anti-PD-1.
bench.model: Human colorectal cancer cells, patient tumour data and in vivo mouse tumours.
bench.result: FOLR1 was a top negative regulator of MHC-I. It was found in tumours but not adjacent normal tissue, and high levels predicted poor response to checkpoint blockade. FOLR1 stabilised AARS1, which lactylated STAT1 and lowered MHC-I. IMGN853 plus anti-PD-1 caused strong tumour regression in vivo.
bench.limitations: Mouse and cell models only. The abstract gives no numbers, and FOLR1 is uneven across tumours, so many patients may not qualify.
bench.meaning: An existing drug class could be tested to help immunotherapy in FOLR1-positive colorectal cancer, if the mouse result holds in people.

diagram.caption: In colorectal cancer models, FOLR1 sets off a chain that lowers MHC-I, so T cells fail to see the tumour.

terms.def: Surface proteins that show fragments of a cell's proteins to killer T cells.
A drug in which an antibody delivers a toxic payload to cells carrying a chosen target.
A chemical tag from lactate that can change how a protein works.
Treatment that releases the brakes on T cells so they attack tumours.

sources.label: Science Translational Medicine, Chen et al.

bench.forYou: Antibody-drug conjugate delivery and immune evasion mechanisms relevant to combination therapy.

bench.title: NIR-II thermoelectric nanoplatform for metabolic reprogramming-enhanced cuproptosis in uterine tumors
bench.headline: A copper-based framework nanomaterial turns 1064 nm laser light into heat, a built-in electric field and copper-driven cell death in uterine tumour models.
bench.authors: Lu X, Zhang L, Yi R, et al.

evidence.model: Uterine (endometrial and cervical) tumour models, details not read
evidence.limitation: Preclinical, read from the abstract only. Group sizes, doses and the exact models were not checked.

bench.question: Can a nanomaterial use second near-infrared light for both heat and electric catalysis to kill uterine tumour cells?
bench.approach: The team built a conductive copper metal-organic framework (CuHPT). Under 1064 nm light, heat gradients create a thermoelectric field (the Seebeck effect) that boosts reactive oxygen species. The framework also releases copper ions.
bench.model: Uterine tumour cells and tumour models (the abstract does not detail them).
bench.result: The abstract reports exceptional photothermal conversion efficiency and more reactive oxygen species. Copper release raised oxidative phosphorylation and primed cells for cuproptosis, and treatment matured dendritic cells and shifted macrophages to the M1 type. No numbers are given.
bench.limitations: No numbers in the abstract. Fertility preservation is a motivation, not a result, and nothing was tested in people.
bench.meaning: It shows one way to combine light, heat and metal-driven cell death, a design idea for nanophototherapy, pending full data.

terms.def: The second near-infrared light window, about 1000 to 1700 nm, which penetrates tissue deeper than visible light.
The creation of an electric voltage across a material when one side is hotter than the other.
A form of cell death caused by copper building up and clumping certain mitochondrial proteins.
A porous crystal built from metal ions joined by organic molecules.

bench.forYou: NIR-II photothermal agents, light-driven catalysis and metal-ion cell death relevant to nanomedicine design.

method.title: Long-term neutrophil depletion and brain neutrophil analysis in an Alzheimer's mouse
method.gist: A Bio-protocol paper describes how to keep neutrophils low for six weeks in 5xFAD mice, and how to recover and count the neutrophils in the brain.
method.useWhen: You want to test what neutrophils do in an Alzheimer's mouse model and need to check depletion in blood and count neutrophils in brain tissue.

steps.title: Deplete neutrophils
steps.text: Inject anti-Ly6G antibody into the abdomen (intraperitoneally) for six weeks in 5xFAD mice.

steps.title: Escalate the dose
steps.text: Raise the dose over time, because neutrophil regeneration increases the longer depletion lasts.

steps.title: Check blood
steps.text: Monitor depletion in blood by flow cytometry, using an antibody panel designed to avoid interference from the depleting anti-Ly6G clone.

steps.title: Process the brain
steps.text: Combine mechanical dissociation with Percoll density gradient centrifugation to collect brain-infiltrating neutrophils.

steps.title: Analyse by flow cytometry
steps.text: Run flow cytometry on the neutrophils isolated from the brain.

pitfalls: A fixed dose may lose effect over six weeks, so the protocol raises it over time.
The detection antibody can be blocked by the depleting clone, so use the panel the protocol describes.
Doses, timings and gating are not listed here. Take every setting from the protocol.
method.safety: Follow your institution's rules and approvals for animal work, and its safety rules for biological material and centrifuges.

terms.def: The most common white blood cell, a first responder of the immune system.
A mouse strain carrying five human gene variants that cause fast amyloid build-up, used to model Alzheimer's disease.
A technique that counts and sorts single cells as they pass a laser, using fluorescent labels.
A density medium in which spinning a sample separates cell types by how heavy they are.

method.forYou: Immune cell depletion and tissue-recovery workflow that transfers to tumour immunology.

learn.question: What is a network meta-analysis, and what can it say that single trials cannot?
learn.answer: It pools many trials into one web, so that treatments never tested head to head can still be compared. Its answer is only as strong as the trials and links behind it.
learn.analogy: Like ranking chess players who never met: you compare them through the opponents they both played.
body: Most trials compare one drug with placebo. A network meta-analysis links trials that share a treatment, for example drug A against placebo and drug B against placebo, to estimate A against B indirectly.

Results come as an effect size for each pair, such as a standardised mean difference, which puts different symptom scales on one scale. Tools such as CINeMA then grade how much to trust each comparison.
In today's OCD analysis, 52 trials gave clomipramine a high-certainty edge over placebo in adults. Many other comparisons, especially in children, were rated low or very low.

diagram.caption: A network meta-analysis links trials through shared treatments, ranks the drugs, then grades how certain each comparison is.

terms.def: An estimate of A against B built from A against placebo and B against placebo.
Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis, a framework that rates how certain each comparison in a network is.
An inactive treatment given to a control group.

sources.label: The Lancet Psychiatry, Cohen et al. (OCD network meta-analysis)

trials.title: Lithium orotate 10 mg daily in Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment
trials.what: A newly registered randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study lasting 18 months, planning 200 participants. The primary outcomes are a 2-point change in the MMSE memory score and a clock drawing test.
trials.who: People with Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment, randomised 1:1 to lithium orotate or matching placebo.

curiosity.title: A brain that copes well with Alzheimer's can hide it
curiosity.gist: Around a third of older people with no dementia have Alzheimer's plaques at autopsy. Researchers call this resilience, but it can delay diagnosis.
body: In The Conversation, a researcher explains that resilient brains carry amyloid and tau yet keep thinking well. In one form, cells are lost but symptoms stay quiet, so a person can seem well while the brain shrinks.

Women on average have better verbal memory, which the tests for Alzheimer's lean on, so signs may be missed. People with high cognitive reserve show symptoms later but then decline faster. The article suggests resilience may also blur drug trials, since resilient people decline slowly on drug or placebo.

evidence.limitation: An expert article, not a study. The studies it cites were not read, and it is not a diagnostic guide.

terms.def: The brain's ability to adapt and keep working well despite ageing or disease, built by education and mental activity.
A protein that builds up as plaques between brain cells in Alzheimer's disease.
A protein that forms tangles inside brain cells in Alzheimer's disease.
